stages.title: SUBORDINATE ENRICHMENT — ONLY AFTER THE COMPLETE CORE

pills.text: PURE RESEARCH ALONE DOES NOT CREATE BIOMANUFACTURING CAPABILITY.
BIOTECHNOLOGY POLICY MUST BALANCE OPEN SCIENTIFIC PROGRESS WITH PRODUCT
SECTORAL PROGRESS OFTEN DEPENDS ON CHALLENGE CALLS
INCUBATORS AND FOCUSED TRANSLATIONAL PROGRAMMES RATHER THAN FRAGMENTED GRANTS.

groups.heading: OPTIONAL SCIENTIFIC / ENGINEERING DEPTH
items: CAUTION: Science funding versus translation funding: pure research alone does not create biomanufacturing capability.
CAUTION: Public-good science versus commercial IP: biotechnology policy must balance open scientific progress with product incentives.
CAUTION: Mission-mode governance: sectoral progress often depends on challenge calls,
incubators and focused translational programmes rather than fragmented grants.

groups.heading: READINESS, UNIT OR STATUS LIMIT
items: CAUTION: Biosafety and quality oversight: fast innovation cannot bypass safety, validation and ethical scrutiny.
CAUTION: Biotechnology matters for health security, sustainable industry, climate-friendly production and agricultural resilience.
CAUTION: Biomanufacturing can generate high-value domestic production without replicating traditional heavy-industry logic.
CAUTION: India’s comparative advantage could lie in linking scientific manpower, cost-efficient development and mission-mode public support.

groups.heading: COMPARATIVE TECHNOLOGY / GOVERNANCE NUANCE
items: CAUTION: Scale-up gap: many promising biological ideas fail between benchtop and pilot plant.
CAUTION: Infrastructure gap: biofoundries, test facilities and GMP-quality manufacturing are expensive and specialised.
CAUTION: Regulatory uncertainty: product categories spanning food, agriculture, health and environment can face multiple regulators.
CAUTION: Financing gap: long gestation and technical failure risk can deter private capital.
